questions.title: Package manager
questions.context: CLAUDE.md/PROJECT.md do not specify a package manager. Next 16 defaults to npm in docs but the ecosystem has shifted. Whatever you pick locks the lockfile, CI cache, and Vercel build command. Greenfield repo — no prior lockfile to honor.

options.label: pnpm
options.description: Fast, disk-efficient via content-addressed store. Strict peer deps catch bugs early. Vercel + GitHub Actions both have first-class caching. Ecosystem standard for new Next projects in 2026.

options.label: npm
options.description: Zero-config, ships with Node. Simplest CI, no extra install step. Slower installs and looser dep resolution than pnpm but maximally vanilla.

options.label: bun
options.description: Fastest installs + built-in test runner. Still has rough edges with some Node-native packages (notably `postgres-js` works, but Sentry + some Turbopack paths can be finicky). Higher risk/reward.

questions.title: Node.js version
questions.context: Affects Vercel runtime, GH Actions setup-node, Dockerized Postgres service container compatibility, and local dev parity. Serwist 9, Drizzle 0.45, Next 16 all require ≥18 with modern engines. Vercel currently supports Node 20 and 22 on Pro.

options.label: Node 22 LTS
options.description: Active LTS with modern V8, native test runner, and `--watch` flag. Best balance of stability and modernity for a 2026 project. Vercel-supported.

options.label: Node 20 LTS
options.description: Maintenance LTS through April 2026 (goes EOL mid-project). Safer if you hit any tooling bugs on 22, but risks a forced upgrade mid-build.

options.label: Node 24 (current)
options.description: Latest odd-number release — not LTS. Breaks some Vercel/Supabase-CLI paths historically. Not recommended for production.

questions.title: Linter & formatter
questions.context: Next 16 still scaffolds ESLint + a Next config by default. Biome has eaten much of the lint/format space in 2025-26 and is ~30× faster. Whichever you pick shapes `ci.yml` lint step, editor integration, and pre-commit hooks. No existing config to honor.

options.label: Biome (lint + format in one)
options.description: Single tool, single config file, no Prettier/ESLint plugin juggling. 30× faster in CI. Handles TS/JS/JSON/CSS. Slight gaps vs ESLint for some React-specific rules, mostly closed in 2025.

options.label: ESLint + Prettier (Next default)
options.description: Biggest ecosystem, every rule under the sun, eslint-plugin-react/jsx-a11y/import battle-tested. Slower, two configs, plugin churn. Most tutorials assume this.

options.label: oxlint + Prettier
options.description: Rust-based ESLint-compatible linter, extremely fast. Still missing some rules. Aggressive choice — viable but least mature.

questions.title: Pre-commit git hooks
questions.context: You have a no-ad-hoc-error-codes rule, a banned-imports list (no `next-pwa`, no `pg`, no `date-fns` without `-tz`, no `Sentry.setUser({email})`), and design-system guardrails. These are cheap to enforce as a pre-commit check rather than waiting for CI.

options.label: lefthook
options.description: Config in one YAML, parallel hooks out of the box, no Node dependency. Fastest. Simple config for lint-staged-style file filters.

options.label: husky + lint-staged
options.description: Most common combo in Next projects. More moving parts but every tutorial uses it. Works with any package manager.

options.label: simple-git-hooks
options.description: Minimal — a package.json config, no husky bloat. Less flexible but matches your 'no ceremony' style.

options.label: No local hooks — rely on CI only
options.description: Keep commits fast, let CI be the gate. Risk: slower feedback when lint/typecheck fails, wastes a PR round-trip.

questions.title: Commit message convention
questions.context: Solo-plus-Claude build but eventually a contributor project. GSD workflow already produces structured commits (`docs(01): ...`, `feat(phase): ...`). Question is whether to *enforce* that format with commitlint or leave it as a soft convention.

options.label: Conventional Commits + commitlint (enforced)
options.description: Auto-enforced in pre-commit and CI. Enables auto-changelog and semantic-release later. Matches GSD's own commit style.

options.label: Conventional Commits as convention, not enforced
options.description: Document the format in CONTRIBUTING.md. No tool enforces it. Rely on discipline + GSD workflow commits.

options.label: Freeform
options.description: No convention. Fastest for solo work but makes changelogs manual and loses signal about intent.

questions.title: TypeScript strict flags beyond `strict` + `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`
questions.context: INFRA-01 locks `strict` + `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`. Some teams go further. Each extra flag catches a real class of bug but also rejects patterns that are common in Next/React code (e.g. `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` breaks `Partial<Props>` spreads).

options.label: Strict-plus core (recommended)
options.description: Add `noImplicitOverride`, `noFallthroughCasesInSwitch`, `noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature`, `forceConsistentCasingInFileNames`. Catches real bugs, low friction with React/Next patterns.

options.label: Maximum strict
options.description: Above + `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` + `noImplicitReturns` + `useUnknownInCatchVariables`. Maximum safety, more friction with third-party types (Drizzle, Supabase JS). Expect 10-20% more casts.

options.label: Just `strict` + `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`
options.description: Stay at INFRA-01 minimum. Fastest velocity, accept some preventable classes of bug.

questions.title: Path alias style
questions.context: PRD §2 repo layout uses `src/contexts/{ctx}/{layer}/`. Cross-layer imports will be frequent. Aliases are configured once in tsconfig.json + resolved by Next automatically. No aliases yet since repo is empty.

options.label: `@/*` → `src/*` (Next convention)
options.description: One alias root. Matches every Next tutorial. Imports look like `@/contexts/iam/domain/user.ts`. Simple and portable.

options.label: Per-context aliases
options.description: `@iam/*`, `@catalog/*`, `@shared/*`. More expressive but 8+ aliases to maintain. Enforces context boundaries visually in imports.

options.label: Layered aliases
options.description: `@domain/*`, `@app/*`, `@infra/*`, `@shared/*`. Expresses DDD layering instead of context. Less context discipline.

questions.title: Scaffold empty bounded-context folders in Phase 1?
questions.context: Phase 1's INFRA-02 success criterion says 'bounded-context folder layout from PRD §2 in place'. Phase 2 (Data Layer) is where the folders actually get filled with domain types, repos, adapters. Question: create empty `domain/`, `application/`, `infrastructure/`, `api/`, `inngest/` with `.gitkeep` in Phase 1, or leave until Phase 2?

options.label: Scaffold all empty folders now with README stubs
options.description: Every `src/contexts/{ctx}/{layer}/` gets a placeholder README or .gitkeep explaining what lives there. Phase 1 verifiably satisfies INFRA-02. Phase 2 just fills in the blanks.

options.label: Scaffold only top-level context folders
options.description: Create `src/contexts/iam/`, `src/contexts/catalog/`, etc. — but not the inner layer folders. Phase 2 decides layer folder structure per-context.

options.label: Defer entirely to Phase 2
options.description: Phase 1 only creates `src/shared/` minimal pieces needed for smoke (e.g. error codes, client). Violates strict reading of INFRA-02 — requires rewriting INFRA-02 into Phase 2.

questions.title: Turbopack for production builds
questions.context: Next 16 makes Turbopack the default dev bundler. `next build --turbopack` is opt-in for production in 16.x (stable in 16.2). Your PRD notes 'Turbopack requires post-build source map upload', which means you've already committed to Turbopack somewhere. Confirming scope: dev only, or dev + build?

options.label: Turbopack for dev AND prod build
options.description: `next build --turbopack`. Faster CI builds, aligns with your 'source maps uploaded post-build' note. This is what the PRD implies.

options.label: Turbopack dev, webpack prod build
options.description: Safer — webpack build is the longest-tested path. Slower CI. Source maps still need CI upload since Vercel doesn't auto-upload for webpack builds either when Vercel git integration is OFF.

options.label: Webpack dev AND prod
options.description: Most conservative. Slower local dev iteration. Not recommended given Next 16 defaults.

questions.title: Playwright browser coverage in CI
questions.context: INFRA-23 says Playwright E2E. More browsers = more CI time + more minutes billed. Your target users are Brazilian mobile PWA users (predominantly Android Chrome + iOS Safari). WebKit test catches Safari-isms.

options.label: Chromium only (fastest)
options.description: ~3× faster CI. Covers ~70% of BR mobile traffic. Accept risk on Safari/Firefox quirks, catch them in manual QA. Good for early phases.

options.label: Chromium + WebKit
options.description: Covers iOS Safari PWA — critical for your mobile-first audience. Adds ~40% CI time. Recommended given PWA focus.

options.label: Chromium + WebKit + Firefox
options.description: Full coverage, slowest CI. Firefox is <3% mobile BR. Probably overkill for MVP.

questions.title: Branch protection rules on `main`
questions.context: You're solo-plus-Claude right now. Branch protection prevents force-push and accidental direct merges but adds friction if you need to hotfix. GitHub Free supports basic protection on public + private repos.

options.label: Require PR + required status checks (ci.yml + deploy-preview.yml) + no force-push
options.description: All changes go through PR, CI must pass, no bypass even for admin. Matches 'every PR flows through GitHub Actions' success criterion. Slightly slower for true emergencies.

options.label: Require PR + checks, allow admin bypass
options.description: Same as (a) but you can force-merge in an emergency. Small back door, mostly symbolic protection.

options.label: No branch protection
options.description: Fastest. Relies on discipline. Doesn't match the stated success criterion — would need re-scoping.

questions.title: DB migration runner in CI
questions.context: INFRA-12 says integration tests run against `postgres:16-alpine` with Drizzle migrations seeded. INFRA-13 says deploy-preview applies migrations to Supabase branch DB. Two distinct paths (local container vs Supabase branch). Question: one migration tool for both, or mix?

options.label: `drizzle-kit migrate` for both
options.description: Single source of truth. Drizzle generates + applies migrations from `schema.ts`. Supabase branch DB is just a Postgres URL — drizzle-kit doesn't care. Simpler. Matches INFRA-04 'Drizzle mandatory'.

options.label: `drizzle-kit migrate` for integration tests, `supabase db push` for branch DB
options.description: Supabase CLI handles branch DB as a first-class concept including Auth schema migrations. Cleaner for LGPD/Storage bits that live in Supabase-owned schemas. Two tools to keep in sync.

options.label: Raw SQL via `psql` in CI
options.description: Maximum control, no tooling abstraction. Most verbose CI steps. Not recommended given Drizzle lock-in.

questions.title: Vercel function region
questions.context: Target users are in Brazil. Vercel Pro offers `gru1` (São Paulo) region for serverless functions. Default `iad1` (Virginia) adds ~120ms RTT from BR. Affects every API call including identification (which has a 50s total budget).

options.label: `gru1` (São Paulo) — single region
options.description: Lowest latency for BR users. Matches your locale-first philosophy. Requires Vercel Pro. Cold starts can be slightly slower on less-popular regions.

options.label: `iad1` (Virginia) — default
options.description: Largest pool → fastest cold starts. +~100-150ms latency from BR. Acceptable for most pages, worse for the identification flow.

options.label: Multi-region
options.description: Not supported on Vercel serverless for SSR without Edge runtime. Skip — not a real option for your stack.

questions.title: Integration test DB lifecycle
questions.context: INFRA-23 'zero DB mocking'. Every integration test hits real Postgres. How tests isolate from each other affects speed and determinism.

options.label: Fresh DB per test file, transaction rollback per test
options.description: CI spins up Postgres once, Vitest applies migrations once, each test wraps in a transaction rolled back at the end. Fastest and deterministic. Standard pattern.

options.label: Fresh DB per test suite, truncate between tests
options.description: Truncate is slower than transaction rollback but survives transactional code under test. Use if you test `BEGIN/COMMIT` logic directly.

options.label: Full DB reset between every test
options.description: Slowest. Most isolated. Probably overkill for Phase 1 smoke tests.

questions.title: Sentry trace sample rate for Phase 1
questions.context: Phase 1 only ships a skeleton — no real user traffic. Traces cost money on Sentry paid plans. Errors are free. Sample rate can be raised in later phases once there's real load.

options.label: Errors only, traces 0.0 for Phase 1
options.description: Wire the SDK, only capture exceptions. No performance data. Cheapest. Can flip on later with a env var change.

options.label: Errors + 10% traces (0.1)
options.description: Catches perf regressions from day 1 without breaking the bank. Good for later phases but phase 1 traffic is synthetic.

options.label: Errors + 100% traces (1.0) in preview only
options.description: Full tracing in preview envs, off in prod until there's real traffic. Maximum insight during build-out, zero prod cost.

questions.title: Sentry Session Replay
questions.context: Session Replay records DOM mutations and replays a user's session. Major LGPD risk: default replays capture form inputs, text content, and IPs. LGPD-13 already scrubs Sentry fields. Enabling replay means another surface area to audit.

options.label: Off — do not install Session Replay
options.description: Zero LGPD risk. Matches your strict PII scrubbing posture. Loses visual debugging of frontend bugs. Safest choice.

options.label: On with full masking (`maskAllText`, `blockAllMedia`)
options.description: All text and media redacted in replay. Still need ANPD legal basis review and consent flow updates. Defer until post-launch.

options.label: On without masking
options.description: Not LGPD-compatible given your stance. Do not pick.

questions.title: PostHog initialization gate
questions.context: OBS-02 says PostHog is wired in Phase 1. Under LGPD Art. 7, analytics is typically 'legitimate interest' but user consent is safer. If PostHog initializes before the user grants analytics consent, you fire anonymous `$pageview` events they didn't agree to. Most LGPD-compliant Brazilian apps defer analytics init until consent.

options.label: Defer PostHog init until LGPD analytics consent granted
options.description: SDK loaded but `posthog.opt_out_capturing()` by default; flip to `opt_in_capturing()` on consent. Safest. Misses `signup_completed` event for users who never grant consent but that's acceptable.

options.label: Init with anonymous tracking, identify on consent
options.description: Fire `$pageview` events with a random distinct_id from first load. Identify the user only after they grant consent + verify email. Risk: pre-consent events may be challenged.

options.label: Init immediately and fully
options.description: Most events captured but highest LGPD exposure. Not recommended.

questions.title: PostHog autocapture
questions.context: PostHog autocapture listens to every click/input and sends an event. Opposite philosophy from the curated 14-event taxonomy in OBS-03. Most privacy-conscious apps disable it and emit only the taxonomy events.

options.label: Off — only emit the OBS-03 taxonomy events
options.description: Clean data, predictable volume, LGPD-aligned. Matches the explicit `signup_completed`, `identification_started` etc. taxonomy. Strongly recommended.

options.label: On (PostHog default)
options.description: Captures every click automatically. Easier for ad-hoc analysis later. Harder to predict LGPD exposure. Much larger event volume.

questions.title: Sentry source map upload mechanism
questions.context: Your PRD explicitly calls out 'source maps uploaded post-build from CI because Turbopack requires it'. Two mechanisms: Sentry's Next SDK plugin (auto-upload during build) vs `sentry-cli` in a dedicated GH Actions step. Turbopack affects which works.

options.label: `sentry-cli sourcemaps upload` in deploy-production.yml
options.description: Explicit GH Actions step after `vercel build`. Works regardless of bundler. Matches your PRD note. Releases tagged with `$GITHUB_SHA`.

options.label: `@sentry/nextjs` automatic upload via `withSentryConfig`
options.description: SDK plugin does it during build. Simpler for webpack. Turbopack support was added in Sentry SDK 8+ but can be flaky. Risk of silent upload failures.

options.label: Upload only from production deploy, skip preview
options.description: Halves Sentry quota usage. Preview errors won't have symbolicated stacks. Trade-off for solo-dev budget.

questions.title: CSP (Content-Security-Policy) posture
questions.context: INFRA-18 says 'standard security headers'. CSP is the hardest to get right. Strict nonce-based CSP breaks some Next features (inline bootstrap scripts). Report-only mode lets you observe before enforcing. `connect-src` must allow Sentry, PostHog EU, Supabase URLs.

options.label: Strict nonce-based CSP, enforced from day 1
options.description: Next 16 supports nonce generation in middleware. Highest security. Some friction with third-party scripts. Allowlist PostHog EU, Sentry, Supabase upfront.

options.label: Moderate CSP with `'self'` + explicit allowlists, enforced
options.description: Ship with `default-src 'self'` + specific allowlists for Sentry/PostHog/Supabase/Stripe. No nonces. Simpler, slightly weaker against XSS.

options.label: CSP report-only in preview, enforced in prod after 1 week
options.description: Observe violations via `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only` in preview, then flip to enforcement in prod once you've tuned the allowlist. Pragmatic for first deploy.

questions.title: HSTS configuration
questions.context: HSTS forces HTTPS for N seconds. `preload` submits the domain to browser preload lists (irreversible for ~6 months). Once preloaded, you cannot serve HTTP. Safe for greenfield projects committed to HTTPS.

options.label: max-age 1 year + includeSubDomains + preload
options.description: Standard strong HSTS. Commits you to HTTPS forever on the apex + subdomains. Safe if you have no legacy HTTP services.

options.label: max-age 1 year + includeSubDomains, NO preload
options.description: Strong but reversible. Can be undone by lowering max-age. Recommended for apps still finding their domain structure.

options.label: max-age 6 months, no preload
options.description: Shorter commit. Safer during early development. Upgrade to (a) once domain is stable.

questions.title: Frame embedding policy
questions.context: X-Frame-Options + `frame-ancestors` CSP directive. Stripe checkout may embed your pages in some flows. Plaid-style connectors do too. For a standalone PWA with no embed use case, DENY is safest.

options.label: frame-ancestors 'none' + X-Frame-Options DENY
options.description: No framing allowed. Safest against clickjacking. Standard for standalone PWAs. Stripe doesn't need to frame your pages (you frame theirs).

options.label: frame-ancestors 'self' + X-Frame-Options SAMEORIGIN
options.description: Allow same-origin frames. Only needed if you embed your own routes in iframes. Not currently planned.

questions.title: Error code registry shape
questions.context: INFRA-20 + PRD §5: 'closed registry, no ad-hoc codes'. Codes include `email_unverified`, `consent_required`, `rate_limited`, `validation_failed`, `provider_unavailable`, `cost_ceiling_reached` (internal), `breaker_open` (internal). Shape affects every route handler that emits errors.

options.label: `as const` object + union type
options.description: export const ErrorCode = { EmailUnverified: 'email_unverified', ... } as const; export type ErrorCode = typeof ErrorCode[keyof typeof ErrorCode]; — best ergonomics: literal union types, tree-shakeable, works with Zod. Modern TS standard.

options.label: TS `enum`
options.description: Classic `enum ErrorCode { EmailUnverified = 'email_unverified', ... }`. Simpler syntax but `enum` is mildly discouraged in modern TS (runtime overhead, awkward with `const` modules).

options.label: Zod enum as the source of truth
options.description: Define codes in Zod (`z.enum([...])`), derive TS type from schema. Single source for runtime validation + types. Couples error codes to Zod — acceptable given INFRA-09 already locks Zod.

questions.title: Phase 1 E2E smoke test scope
questions.context: Phase 1 has no features yet. Playwright needs *something* to prove the preview URL + Supabase branch DB + deploy pipeline all work. Too much scope = Phase 1 slips into Phase 3 territory. Too little = pipeline confidence is shaky.

options.label: Home page loads + pt-BR `<html lang>` + no console errors + health route returns 200
options.description: Covers: Next renders, locale config works, middleware runs, DB reachable via a health route that does a simple `SELECT 1`. ~3 assertions. Tight scope.

options.label: Above + Sentry receives a deliberate error + PostHog fires a ping event
options.description: Actually exercises observability end-to-end in preview. Requires test endpoints or test flags. Phase 1's success criterion #4 calls for this.

options.label: Minimal: `/` returns 200 and contains 'Folhário'
options.description: Fastest. Barely proves Next runs. Doesn't exercise DB or middleware. Not enough confidence for a 'foundation' phase.

questions.title: next-intl routing mode
questions.context: next-intl supports URL-prefix routing (`/pt-BR/home`), no-prefix single-locale mode, and a 'default locale without prefix' hybrid. You ship pt-BR only with no planned second locale at launch. Prefix adds SEO/URL noise for no gain.

options.label: Single-locale, no routing, no URL prefix
options.description: `setRequestLocale('pt-BR')` hardcoded, no middleware routing. URLs stay clean (`/home`, not `/pt-BR/home`). Easiest to add a second locale later via middleware swap.

options.label: Prefix-as-needed (default pt-BR has no prefix)
options.description: Middleware routes `/en-US/home` etc. but `/home` serves pt-BR. Slight overhead now for future-proofing.

options.label: Always-prefixed (`/pt-BR/home`)
options.description: Most explicit. Ugliest URLs for a single-locale launch. Skip.

questions.title: Serwist PWA precache scope in Phase 1
questions.context: Phase 1 wires `@serwist/next`. Phase 3 builds the actual app shell + manifest. Question: does Phase 1's SW precache anything real, or is it a no-op shell that proves the wiring works?

options.label: No-op SW in Phase 1 (empty precache manifest, NetworkFirst for everything)
options.description: Just proves Serwist builds and registers. Phase 3 adds real precaching + offline fallback. Minimum viable PWA scaffolding.

options.label: Precache build assets only (Next's auto-generated manifest)
options.description: Serwist's default `@serwist/next` integration precaches Next's static assets. No offline page, no custom routes. Still safe for Phase 1.

options.label: Full offline shell with manifest + icons in Phase 1
options.description: Scope creep into Phase 3 (Design System & App Shell). Don't do in Phase 1.
